title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 26
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Paid for by Something Else
passages.text:
A. The newspaper was never sold for what it cost to produce. From the point at which printing became cheap enough for daily publication, the cover price covered a fraction of the expense and the remainder came from advertising, which means the reader was never the customer in the sense usually assumed. What was being sold was the reader's attention, and the news was the inducement to supply it.

B. That arrangement had a consequence for content that was visible from the beginning. Advertising rewards volume of readership rather than intensity of interest, so publications drifted towards material with broad appeal and away from material that mattered greatly to a few. The same economics that funded expensive reporting also constrained what kind of reporting could be funded, and both effects came from the same source.

C. Classified advertising deserves separate treatment because it behaved differently from display advertising and mattered more. Notices of jobs, property and goods for sale were placed by people with no interest in the publication's journalism, and produced a stream of revenue almost unrelated to editorial quality. For much of the twentieth century, serious reporting in many countries was funded by people trying to sell second-hand furniture.

D. The internet's effect is frequently described as readers refusing to pay, which misidentifies what happened. Readers had never paid much. What collapsed was the classified revenue, which moved to platforms that did the same job better — searchable, current, cheaper and unbundled from anything else — and the loss removed the subsidy rather than the audience. Readership in many cases rose while revenue fell.

E. The replacement funding has proved unequal to the same task for structural reasons. Display advertising online is sold through intermediaries at prices far below print equivalents, and rewards quantity of pages viewed, which favours material that is cheap to produce and widely shared. Subscription works for a small number of publications with distinctive national or specialist standing and does not scale to the local level, where the collapse has been most complete.

F. What has been lost is concentrated in a place that generates little attention. Local reporting — councils, courts, planning decisions, procurement — was always cross-subsidised, never popular, and is the layer that has largely gone. Studies of areas that lost their local paper find measurable consequences in civic participation and in the cost of municipal borrowing, which is a strange but telling way for an absence of scrutiny to become visible.

passages.title: Knowing Which Way Is Up
passages.text:
Balance feels like a single sense and is not. Standing upright is maintained by combining information from at least three independent sources: the inner ear, which detects rotation and linear acceleration; vision, which reports the position of the world; and sensors in muscles, joints and the soles of the feet reporting the body's own configuration. The experience is seamless, and the seamlessness conceals a continuous act of reconciliation.

The reconciliation matters because the sources disagree regularly. Vision reports stability when the visual field itself is moving — sitting in a stationary train beside a departing one produces a compelling sensation of movement — and the inner ear reports acceleration in situations where the body is not accelerating at all. The system weights the inputs according to which is currently more reliable, and much of what is interesting about balance appears when that weighting is wrong or when the inputs genuinely conflict.

Motion sickness is the clearest case of conflict, and the leading explanation — one of several competing accounts rather than a settled one — is unsettling in its implications. Below deck on a ship, the inner ear reports motion while vision reports a stationary cabin, and this particular combination — internal signals of movement without corresponding visual evidence — is also produced by certain toxins that affect the nervous system. The response, on this account, is a defensive one that evolved for poisoning and is triggered inappropriately by transport.

Age changes the calculation in a way that explains a great deal of injury. All three systems degrade with age, and their degradation is gradual and unnoticed because the remaining systems compensate. The compensation conceals the loss until a situation removes one of the remaining inputs — a dark room, an uneven surface, a turned head — and the person falls. Falls are usually recorded as accidents when they are more accurately the point at which an accumulated deficit becomes visible.

The practical consequence is that balance is trainable, which is not widely understood. Deliberately practising in conditions that reduce one input — standing on an unstable surface, closing the eyes, moving the head — improves the weighting the system performs, and trials of such training in older adults show reductions in falls that compare favourably with any drug intervention for the same purpose. The training is unglamorous, requires no equipment and is prescribed far less often than medication.

The wider lesson concerns how confidently the body reports on itself. The sense of one's own position feels direct and certain, and it is in fact a construction assembled from disagreeing sources and continuously revised. Illusions of balance are not malfunctions but glimpses of the assembly process, and the confidence attached to the resulting experience is not a measure of its accuracy.

passages.title: What a Degree Is For
passages.text:
The financial return to a university degree is real, substantial on average, and almost useless as a guide to any individual decision. Average figures combine fields with returns that differ by more than the gap between having a degree and not having one, institutions whose graduates differ mainly in who they admitted, and students who completed with students who did not. A statistic assembled from populations that heterogeneous can be accurate and still tell a particular applicant almost nothing.

Separating what a degree does from what it signals is the central analytical problem and is unresolved. On one account, education adds capability that employers pay for; on another, it identifies people who already had the qualities employers want, and the qualification functions as a filter rather than a transformation. The truth is a mixture in proportions that differ by field, and the practical difference matters: if signalling dominates, expanding enrolment raises the qualification required for the same jobs without raising anyone's productivity.

Evidence for that inflation is easier to find than its defenders acknowledge. Occupations that once recruited school leavers now require degrees without the work having changed, and the requirement often rises fastest where applicants are most plentiful. This is rational for each employer as a screening device and collectively produces a longer and more expensive path to the same position, paid for by the applicant.

The variance that averages conceal is where the actual risk sits. A student who completes a degree with strong demand in the labour market has made an excellent investment; a student who borrows the same amount and does not complete has the debt and none of the return, and non-completion rates at some institutions are high enough that the expected value of enrolling there is genuinely unclear. Systems that publish returns by institution and field rather than in aggregate change applicant behaviour measurably.

The non-financial returns are real and are systematically treated as decoration. Health, civic participation, reported life satisfaction and the intellectual content of the years themselves are not incidental to what a university is for, and reducing the institution to an earnings-generating mechanism concedes an argument that need not be conceded. These returns are, however, distributed similarly to the financial ones and cannot substitute for them in a decision about borrowing.

The policy question that follows is about who bears the risk rather than who receives the benefit. A system funded by student borrowing places the risk on the individual, at the age when they have least information and least capacity to bear a bad outcome; a system funded publicly places it on the taxpayer and is defended by the collective returns that education generates. Most countries have chosen a mixture, and the arguments about proportion are about risk allocation whether or not they are conducted in those terms.
